September CPI report: What to expect Skip Navigation Markets Pre-Markets U.S. Markets Currencies Prediction Markets Cryptocurrency Futures & Commodities Bonds Funds & ETFs Business Economy Finance Health & Science Media Real Estate Energy Climate Transportation Investigations Industrials Retail Wealth Sports Life Small Business Investing Personal Finance Fintech Financial Advisors Options Action ETF Street Buffett Archive Earnings Trader Talk Tech Cybersecurity AI Enterprise Internet Media Mobile Social Media CNBC Disruptor 50 Tech Guide Politics & Policy White House Policy Defense Congress Expanding Opportunity Video Latest Video Full Episodes Livestream Live Audio Live TV Schedule CNBC Podcasts CEO Interviews CNBC Documentaries Digital Originals Watchlist Investing Club Trust Portfolio Analysis Trade Alerts Meeting Videos Homestretch Jim's Columns Education Subscribe PRO Pro News Josh Brown Mike Santoli Calls of the Day My Portfolio Livestream Full Episodes Stock Screener Market Forecast Options Investing Chart Investing Subscribe Livestream Menu Make It select USA INTL Livestream Search quotes, news & videos Livestream Watchlist SIGN IN Create free account Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Economy The latest inflation data is expected to show price increases are accelerating Published Tue, Oct 13 2026 2:05 PM EDT Alex Harring @alex_harring WATCH LIVE Key Points Economists expect the consumer price index for September to rise 0.6% on the month and 3.6% year over year. Core CPI is forecast to show a 0.2% gain on the month and 2.5% annual increase. Oil-related prices could drive the headline figure even higher, one economist warned. Customers shop at a grocery store on Sept. 10, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. Scott Olson | Getty Images Wednesday's closely watched reading on consumer prices could show intensifying inflationary pressures as energy costs keep climbing. Economists polled by Dow Jones expect the headline consumer price index for September to rise 0.6% for the month and to increase 3.6% compared with a year ago. That 12-month number would signal that the rate of price growth is accelerating and moving further from the Federal Reserve 's goal of 2%. So-called core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, is expected to increase 0.2% from August and 2.5% on a 12-month basis. While that would mark a slight slowdown from the prior month, it would be an uptick in year-over-year inflation. Upside risk Oil-related prices could drive the headline figure even higher, said Joe Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM, a tax firm. Energy costs have been among the biggest drivers of inflation since the U.S. war with Iran began earlier this year. President Donald Trump last week announced loosened diesel restrictions on Russia in a bid to juice the global oil trade, though analysts don't believe it will meaningfully bring down prices. Prices for Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, climbed more than 14% in September, bringing its third-quarter advance to about 42%. Brent prices on Tuesday traded around $105 per barrel. "We've got real upside risk on the September CPI," Brusuelas said. "Typically, when we have these moves in inflation, everyone's models undershoot the actual outcome." Sticky oil prices could also push up costs for items in other, non-energy categories, according to Robert Sockin, chief U.S. economist at asset manager PGIM. In this scenario, it would become harder for the Fed to write off the energy prices surge as a short-term shock that won't necessitate interest rate increases. After announcing its first increase in three years last month, the Federal Reserve signaled in its minutes from that meeting that it will likely have to hike rates again . Fed funds futures traders anticipate the central bank will next lift rates at its December policy meeting, according to CME's FedWatch tool. "The list of reasons to hike rates in our view is long," Sockin said. "Ultimately, we have low confidence in the timing of the Fed's next move, but more conviction on the direction of travel." Wednesday's release is the last reading on CPI before November's midterm elections , which could determine whether the Republican party will keep total control in Washington. Economic confidence across political affiliation has fallen this year, according to the University of Michigan's consumer sentiment data. Compared with Democrats, Republican and independent voters have posted steeper declines in sentiment since the start of 2026, the data shows. Economists forecast that the producer price index, a gauge of inflation facing wholesalers due on Thursday, will rise 0.6% from August to September and 5.5% on a 12-month basis. Both of those numbers would mark a modest acceleration in growth compared with August's release.
